pr_title: sql: wrap CastExpr within IndirectionExpr in a ParenExpr
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/issues/63097.

When we type check ParenExpr, we remove the parentheses.
This can cause issues for IndirectionExprs.

For example, something like `('{a}'::_typ)[1]` would
turn into `'{a}'::_typ[1]` after type checking, resulting
in the `[1]` being interpreted as part of the type.
This would result in errors when trying to use these
expressions in default expressions.
This patch checks for this specific case, and if
it finds that there is a CastExpr within an IndirecionExpr,
it will wrap it in a ParenExpr.

Release note: None
pr_comments: This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/cockroachdb/cockroach/63103)

I don't know how to reason about the two approaches. It seems like we decided to format the operator exprs so as to not think about precedence here. One interesting thing is that cast is the highest precedence operator, higher even than the subscripting, *but* I think our problem here is not so much the precedence as the parsing ambiguity. I could be wrong. I wonder if @knz has feelings on this.
@rafiss or @otan if y'all have any insights, they would be appreciated!

> An alternative approach would be to make a cast an `operatorExpr`. I think the below patch will work but may introduce parens in a bunch of places. It'd be nice to find out.

@ajwerner tried out your approach, and it did seem to introduces a lot of additional parens (see the test failures in the CI).

> Hmm, how about this for another take:

Yeah this one passes CI (the one test failure looks completely unrelated).
Cool. That's my preference. The idea is that we're encoding precedence inside the formatting of the AST. Thanks for picking this up.
I think this would benefit from a backport to the stable release branch(es)

issue_context.title: Parentheses are incorrectly removed for type arrays in default expressions
issue_context.body:
**Describe the problem**

The way we currently serialize type arrays in default expressions removes parentheses in the expression. As a result, the expressions becomes invalid and results in an error.

**To Reproduce**

```
CREATE TYPE default_abc AS ENUM('a', 'b', 'c');
CREATE TABLE t (i STRING DEFAULT ('{a}'::_default_abc)[1]::STRING);

ERROR: at or near ":": syntax error
SQLSTATE: 42601
DETAIL: source SQL:
SET ROW ('{a}':::STRING::@100060[1:::INT8]::STRING)
                                  ^
HINT: try \h SET SESSION
```

**Expected behavior**
This syntax should be valid and not result in an error.
The expression should instead be serialized as `('{a}':::STRING::@100060)[1:::INT8]::STRING` (notice the parentheses around `'{a}':::STRING::@100060`, which are currently being dropped).
comments:
Eric points out that  the problem is that we drop all parents in type checking:

> I think it happens here, during the type checking of ParenExpr: https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/9110a1b9f95bd93f4c571bb3190d1eacaf903f8a/pkg/sql/sem/tree/type_check.go#L1236-L1247
It basically just drops the parentheses and only returns the inner expr. There’s even a comment that says Parentheses are semantically unimportant and can be removed/replace

> git blame says that it used to return the entire expression (including the parentheses if i’m not mistaken)
https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/commit/7a02e3aad6e14ba34960063c029436a09967cd07#diff-b2a517db9d4d185d9e0258c[…]33c9277cdc6ba71ebbd95071L606

Unfortunately this seems too simplistic. It seems like any `[...]` tokens after a type get interpreted as part of the type. This is true in postgres too:

```
postgres=# CREATE TYPE typ AS ENUM ('a');
CREATE TYPE
postgres=# SELECT '{a}'::VARCHAR::_typ[1]::VARCHAR;
ERROR:  type "_typ[]" does not exist
postgres=# SELECT ('{a}'::VARCHAR::_typ)[1]::VARCHAR;
 varchar 
---------
 a
 ```

In short, it does seem like these parens are meaningful in this case. I wonder if there are other cases we haven't thought of? For now, one thing we can do is look and see if the outermost expression is a cast and retain the parens.
Another option is to let the `ParensExpr` remove itself but then inject parens in the case where you've got a cast expr in an indirection expr then you need to wrap it in a `ParensExpr`

review_comments:
interesting, my preference would have been to always wrap CastExpr with parens in `exprFmtWithParen` but too bad that seems to break things...

i don't know if i'm ready to advocate for this yet but: what if we _always_ wrap the inner expr of an IndirectionExpr with parens...? just curious how noisy that gets and if there are major downsides
